resources.string: The greatest and finest sanctuary of ancient Athens, dedicated primarily to its patron, the goddess Athena, dominates the centre of the modern city from the rocky crag known as the Acropolis. The most celebrated myths of ancient Athens, its greatest religious festivals, earliest cults and several decisive events in the city\'s history are all connected to this sacred precinct. The monuments of the Acropolis stand in harmony with their natural setting and combine different orders and styles of Classical art in a most innovative manner and have influenced art and culture for many centuries. The Acropolis of the fifth century BC is the most accurate reflection of the splendour, power and wealth of Athens at its greatest peak, the golden age of Perikles. Athenians and foreigners alike worked on this project, receiving a salary of one drachma a day. The most important buildings visible on the Acropolis today - that is, the Parthenon, the Propylaia, the Erechtheion and the temple of Athena Nike, were erected during this period under the supervision of the greatest architects, sculptors and artists of their time. The temples on the north side of the Acropolis housed primarily the earlier Athenian cults and those of the Olympian gods, while the southern part of the Acropolis was dedicated to the cult of Athena in her many qualities: as Polias (patron of the city), Parthenos, Pallas, Promachos (goddess of war), Ergane (goddess of manual labour) and Nike (Victory). After the end of the Peloponnesian war in 404 BC and until the first century BC no other important buildings were erected on the Acropolis.

The Albaicín, also known as Albayzín (from Arabic: ٱلْبَيّازِينْ, romanized: al-Bayyāzīn), is a district of Granada, in the autonomous community of Andalusia, Spain. It is centered around a hill on the north side of the Darro River which passes through the city. The neighbourhood is notable for its historic monuments and for largely retaining its medieval street plan dating back to the Nasrid period (13th to 15th centuries), although it nonetheless went through many physical and demographic changes after the end of the Reconquista in 1492. It was declared a World Heritage Site in 1994, as an extension of the historic site of the nearby Alhambra.

Amathus is one of the significant ancient city-kingdoms of Cyprus where, according to mythology, Greek hero Theseus left the pregnant Ariadne to be attended by local women. It was also an important site of worship of the Goddess Aphrodite. There are various archaeological finds at the site, including the Agora, the public baths, the Temple of Aphrodite, early Christian basilicas and several tombs. The Agora is located in the lower town. In ancient times, it was the traditional hub for commercial and political activities, and the buildings surrounding it, played an important role in the daily life of the city.

The Fontana Maggiore in Perugia was once fed by this Roman aqueduct. The aqueduct was built in 1245 and it was an extraordinary work: without using pumps, it was still able to bring water to a steep and uneven city like Perugia. It is about 4km long. In the middle of 1800s, the aqueduct stopped its work as it was too expensive. Today, still, it offers one of the most beautiful promenades in Italy. The most characteristic part is from Porta Sant\'Angelo (near the Cathedral and the Fontana Maggiore) with a bridge supported by a dozen bays with large arches and low, colourful houses.

The Archaeological Museum of Patras is one of the most important museums in the country. It was built in 2008 to designs by architect Theofanis Bobotis. The impressive building of the museum is located at the northern entrance of the city and is a model of architectural elegance. Its exterior, in complete harmony with the surrounding area, charms every passerby. A spherical dome covered with titanium sheets dominates an artificial lake, signifying the relationship of the city of Patras with the liquid element. It has a total area of 5,955 square metres and has three large halls for the permanent exhibition, one hall for temporary exhibitions, modern reception and public service areas, an amphitheatre, a refreshment room, conservation laboratories, storage rooms for antiquities and an open-air area, which also serves as a parking area for visitors\' vehicles. The three halls with their respective sections shed light on the burial customs, private and public life of the people of antiquity. The permanent exhibition follows the display mode of all modern museums in the world, i.e. many of the exhibits are not enclosed in cases, but stand freely in the space. Panoramic routes allow you to tour the museum in a short time, while modern technology (virtual museum) allows you to communicate with other cultural sites around the world. In addition, continuous projections on video walls within the exhibition space complement the exhibits. The highly dynamic design of the exhibition and the way the objects are projected will capture your attention and stimulate your interest in learning.

Athens has been the capital of Greece since 1834 and is the country\'s largest and most densely populated city. The Athens basin, including Piraeus, has a population of 3,059,764 inhabitants. The name of the city of Athens comes from the patron goddess Athena. It is located in Attica, in eastern Central Greece, and is one of the oldest cities in the world, with its recorded history dating back to 3,200 BC. The legacy of the classical era is still evident in the city, represented by ancient monuments and works of art, the most famous of which is the Parthenon, considered an emblematic monument of ancient Western civilization. Roman and Byzantine monuments still remain in the city, as well as a small number of Ottoman monuments, while in its historical core there are elements that reflect the historical continuity of the city.
Basílica de Nuestra Señora del Pilar

According to a very old tradition, the Basilica was built over the pillar on which the Virgin Mary leaned at the moment of her apparition to Saint James on 2nd January 40 AD. This is why the Basilica is one of the most important Marian centers in the world. The Basilica you see now is not the one built after the legend but, due to fires and demolitions, the present one dates back to the end of the 17th century. The four towers are called: Torre de Santiago (the oldest), Nuestra Señora del Pilar, Torre de San Francisco de Borja, and its bride Torre Leonor de Salas.

The Camino de Santiago, also known as the Way of St. James, is a renowned pilgrimage of medieval origin that sees pilgrims’ journey to the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Galicia in the northwest of Spain. Legend has it that the remains of the Apostle St. James the Great were buried in the Cathedral and discovered by a shepherd in the 9th century. The city of Santiago is named after St. James: Santiago de Compostela means St. James of the Field of Stars. If you’re a history buff, make sure you discover the history of the Camino. Due to the enduring popularity of the Camino de Santiago and the many Camino routes, they have been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993.

The castle, built in Aragonese style, has a central tower and two lower round side towers, crenellated and equipped with buckles. King Ferdinand II of Naples promised the Materrani that the town would no longer be ceded to feudal lords. Count Giovani Carlo Tramontano, entrusted with the county in 1946, imposed heavy taxes to fund the castle\'s construction (25,000 ducats). The castle overlooked the city from a hill, aimed at controlling surrounding land rather than defending the city. Disgruntled citizens staged a coup against the Count, leaving the castle unfinished. Some restoration was done in 2008, making it an ideal venue for cultural and musical events.

The origin of Castrocucco Castle is shrouded in mystery, possibly dating back to the 9th century, as mentioned in a 1079 bull by Alfano I, bishop of Salerno. Some historians link it to the defense of the ancient Greek city Blanda Julia, which later became Matera. Abandoned in the 17th century, the castle\'s condition is deteriorating, yet remnants of the enclosure walls, about twenty buildings, a watchtower, and the Church of San Pietro with crypts and ancient paintings are still distinguishable. Its strategic perch defended against sea-borne Saracen raids, protecting both the area and Maratea. Although under the Ministry of Cultural Heritage\'s protection since 2005, locals seek restoration to preserve this historical gem.

The Granada Cathedral, also known as the Cathedral of the Incarnation, is an impressive religious monument located in the city of Granada, Spain. Built in the Renaissance style, it combines both Gothic and Renaissance elements. Construction began in 1523 and lasted for over 180 years. The facade stands out with its stone details and sculptures. The interior is vast and filled with religious art and ornate decorations. The Royal Chapel houses the tombs of the Catholic Monarchs, Queen Isabella I and King Ferdinand II. The bell tower offers panoramic views of the city and the Alhambra. It is an important cultural and religious symbol of Granada.

The Santiago de Compostela Arch Cathedral Basilica (Spanish and Galician: Catedral Basilica de Santiago de Compostela) is part of the Metropolitan Archdiocese of Santiago de Compostela and is an integral component of the Santiago de Compostela World Heritage Site in Galicia, Spain. The cathedral is the reputed burial place of Saint James the Great, one of the apostles of Jesus Christ. It is also among the remaining churches in the world built over the tomb of an apostle, the other ones being St Peter\'s Basilica in Vatican City, St Thomas Cathedral Basilica, Chennai in India and Basilica of St. John in Izmir, Turkey.
La Catedral del Salvador en su Epifanía (SEO)

The Cathedral of the Savior in its Epiphany of Zaragoza, was the first cathedral of the city of Zaragoza. It was built on the remains of the ancient Roman Forum of Caesaraugusta, above the Visigothic church and above the ancient Great Mosque of Saraqusta, so that today we can see an incredible combination of styles, from Romanesque to neoclassical. Attached to the SEO, there is the most photographed wall of the city (it has been declared a World Heritage Site by Unesco), it is part of the Parish Church of St. Michael the Archangel. It was built in 1374 and is composed of several parts in masonry, masonry, porticoes, ceramics and decorations of bright colors.
The Statue of the Christ the Redeemer

The Carrara marble statue of Christ the Redeemer is 21 meters high, with a 19-meter span, placed atop a mountain near Santuario di San Biagio. Preserving relics since 732 AD, it\'s Italy\'s tallest and Europe\'s third-largest Christ statue. In 1963, Count Stefano Rivetti di Valcervo commissioned the statue inspired by Rio de Janeiro\'s Christ the Redeemer. Sculpted by Bruno Innocenti, Maratea\'s Christ is younger and more cheerful, with raised arms at a 45-degree angle and a unique face. It replaced a 1907 war memorial, honoring lives lost during the 1806 invasion of Naples. The statue symbolizes the region\'s history and Christian culture.
Church of Panagia (Our Lady) tou Moutoulla

The Panagia of Moutoulla is a small orthodox Christian church of the Frankish period in Cyprus. It is located on the southern outskirts of the mountainous village of Moutoullas (Nicosia District), in the mountains of Marathasa of the Troodos mountain range. Built, according to the foundational inscription, in 1280 in the type of the road-roofed church and decorated with frescoes that continue the older carved tradition and incorporate western influences, the Panagia of Moutoullas is an important example of late Byzantine architecture and art in Cyprus. Due to its importance it has been declared a World Heritage Site by UNESCO.

The church of Agios Lazaros is located in the town center, and is one of the most remarkable examples of Byzantine architecture in Cyprus. The church lies over the tomb of the saint. A fire in 1970 damaged much of the interior, including extensive damage to a section of the iconostasis. The iconostasis has been partially restored and was re-plated with gold between 1972 and 1974. During the subsequent renovations of the church, on November 2, 1972, human remains were discovered in a marble sarcophagus under the altar, and were identified as part of the saint\'s relics.

Corfu or Kerkyra is a Greek island in the Ionian Sea, of the Ionian Islands,] and, including its small satellite islands, forms the margin of the northwestern frontier of Greece. The island is part of the Corfu regional unit, and is administered by three municipalities with the islands of Othonoi, Ereikoussa, and Mathraki. The principal city of the island (pop. 32,095) is also named Corfu. Corfu is home to the Ionian University.

The Cyprus Museum is the island’s main and largest archaeological museum and charts the development of Cyprus’ civilization from the Neolithic Age to the Early Byzantine period (7th century). The museum’s collections consist of pottery, jewellery, sculpture, coins, copper objects, and other artifacts, all exhibited in chronological order in the various museum galleries. Pieces typical of Cypriot culture - and of particularly important artistic, archaeological and historical value - include the cross-shaped idol of the Chalcolithic period, Early Bronze Age pottery from Vouni, Late Bronze Age golden jewellery from Egkomi, and the 1st century BC statue of Aphrodite of Soloi.
Fortess of the Sun in Lorca

Along Corso Vannucci, one of the main streets of the city, the top floor of the Priori Palace has housed the National Gallery of Umbria since 1878. The National Gallery hosts one of the most complete, extensive, and richest art collections in the entire region. The artworks are exhibited on the upper floors of Perugia’s Palazzo dei Priori, seat of the City Council since the Middle Ages and the only Italian public building to house a large national museum. The exhibition spaces occupy two floors and the collection comprises the greatest representation of the Umbrian School of painting, ranging from the 13th to the 19th century. The collection is presented in 40 exhibition rooms in the Palazzo. On the second floor of the Gallery, there is an exhibition space for temporary collections, changed several times a year. Here you can appreciate the works of important artists, such as Piero della Francesca, Perugino, and Pintoricchhio, and many others.

Granada, a city in southern Spain, harbors an exceptional cultural heritage in its cobbled streets. With its iconic jewel, the Alhambra, a Moorish palace with stunning gardens and Arab architecture, contrasting with the majesty of the Renaissance-style Cathedral. Its historical neighborhoods, like the Albaicín, preserve the essence of its Moorish and medieval past. The Muslim influence is reflected in the gastronomy, while the Cathedral of Granada, a masterpiece of Spanish Renaissance, stands out for its architectural splendor. Granada is also a melting pot of culture, with festivals, flamenco, and a bohemian atmosphere that inspires artists and poets. An enriching legacy that captivates all visitors.

Piazza IV Novembre is a square in the historic center of Perugia, the capital city of the Umbria region. The asymmetrical square opens up to the convergence of the five road axes that structure the medieval city and for its scenography it has represented in every era the privileged place of urban functions: here the ancient forum was located and there are preserved monuments connected to the system urban planning of the Etruscan-Roman city. This is the most important square in the city of Perugia, where you will find the Fontana Maggiore (the central fountain), the Priori Palace and the Cathedral of San Lorenzo.

Castillo de Jumilla is a historical fortress located in Jumilla, in the region of Murcia, Spain. The castle has a long history, dating back to the medieval period when it served as a defensive fortification. The castle\'s architecture reflects a combination of Medieval and Renaissance styles. It is situated on a little hill next to the town of Jumilla. Its structure includes defensive walls, towers, and other features commonly found in fortified castles. Over time, the castle underwent restoration efforts to preserve its value. It is now open to visitors. The castle often hosts exhibitions, and guided tours, cultural events.

The Arch of Galerius or Kamara and the Rotunda are neighbouring early 4th-century AD monuments in the city of Thessaloniki, in the region of Central Macedonia in northern Greece. As an outstanding example of early Byzantine art and architecture, in addition to the importance of the Rotunda as one of the earliest Christian monuments in the Eastern Roman Empire, both sites were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List n 1988 as part of the Paleochristian and Byzantine monuments of Thessaloniki.

Kourion was an important ancient Greek city-state on the southwestern coast of Cyprus. The earliest evidence of settlement in the broader area of Kourion dates to the Neolithic period (5500-3900 B.C.), whilst the most ancient remains in the general area of the ancient city are associated with settlements and tombs of the Middle and Late Bronze Age. The most important monuments at the site are: The Agora, the House of Achilles, the House of the Gladiators, the Theatre, the Baths and the Complex of Eustolios, the Early Christian Basilica, the Sanctuary of Apollo Hylates, the Stadium, and the Small Basilica.

The Granada Cathedral, also known as the Cathedral of the Incarnation, is an impressive religious monument located in the city of Granada, Spain. Built in the Renaissance style, it combines both Gothic and Renaissance elements. Construction began in 1523 and lasted for over 180 years. The facade stands out with its stone details and sculptures. The interior is vast and filled with religious art and ornate decorations. The Royal Chapel houses the tombs of the Catholic Monarchs, Queen Isabella I and King Ferdinand II. The bell tower offers panoramic views of the city and the Alhambra. It is an important cultural and religious symbol of Granada.

Larnaka is a city on the southeast coast of Cyprus. It is the successor city of ancient Kitio, one of the important points of ancient Cyprus, birthplace among others of the ancient philosopher Zeno. Today it is the third largest city in Cyprus. Larnaka has an international airport, the main and largest airport in Cyprus. It is considered by many to be the most natural and the most beautiful city in Cyprus with 2 natural lakes (Aliki and Lake Oroklinis) but also with an abundance of monuments.

Larnaka Castle was constructed to defend the southern coast of Cyprus and the harbor town of Larnaka and was later used as an artillery station, prison, and a museum. By the 18th century the castle started losing importance and was abandoned. Throughout British rule the castle was used as a prison where they installed gallows to execute prisoners. The last execution took place in 1948. During the Cypriot civil war Greek Cypriots held the castle and they too used it as a prison. After Cypriot independence the castle was converted into a museum.

Larnaka District Archaeological Museum houses a large collection of archaeological finds from the whole district of Larnaka. Exhibits include artifacts from the Neolithic period, the Copper Era and the Archaic, Classical, Hellenistic and Roman periods. Faience (tin-glazed pottery), ivory and alabaster pieces showcase Cyprus’ commercial and international ties with different countries during antiquity. Aside from the large collection of local exhibits, the museum also displays some unique items of Egyptian, Mycenaean, Phoenician, Assyrian and Persian origin that were found in the region of Larnaka, but may have been imported from the other great civilizations of antiquity close to the island.

Limassol is the second largest city in Cyprus and the southernmost in Europe. Its population amounts to 100,952 inhabitants within the municipal limits and to approximately 180,000 in the wider urban area. Known among the cities of Cyprus for its rich nightlife and cultural tradition, Limassol is also the largest port of the island and one of the largest in the Eastern Mediterranean. It has seen rapid growth, especially after 1974, when the other important port of Cyprus, Famagusta, was lost due to the Turkish invasion.

Limassol Medieval Castle is situated in the center of the town next to the old port. The castle was built in the 13th century on the site of an earlier Byzantine castle and has been converted today into a museum. It is the town\'s most popular sightseeing destination because, according to fame, the castle stands on the site where Richard the Lionheart married Berengaria of Navarre and crowned her Queen of England in 1191. Throughout the years, the fort suffered the assaults of many invaders. Finally, in 1590, the Ottomans rebuilt the fort in its current form.
The Statue of the Christ the Redeemer

The Murgia Materana Park, created in 1990, was originally known as the Parco Regionale Archeologico Storico Naturale delle Chiese Rupestri del Materano (Regional Archaeological Historical Natural Park of the Rock Churches of the Matera Region).

This unique park features soft limestone called and holds significant historical value. It includes Palaeolithic caves like the Bat Cave, Neolithic, Bronze, and Iron Age villages (Murgecchia, Murgia Timone, and Trasanello), showcasing prehistoric human presence, mainly shepherds and herdsmen. The park boasts over 150 rock churches, each with distinct architecture and iconography, dating back to the early Middle Ages. Additionally, it boasts a diverse and wild nature, with approximately 1,200 botanical species, including rare ones.

Τhe New Fortress is located on the north-western part of the Old Town, on the Hill of St Markos, above the old port. It was built with earthworks that were piled up from nearby areas, and lined with carved stones that were collected mainly from the material of the ancient city of Corfu (Paleopolis). Its Gate is decorated with a magnificent relief of the Lion of St. Mark, the emblem of Venice. The New fortress is organised in two levels, the lower and the upper level. On the lower level, which includes a pentagonal salient, an additional salient and the little fort of ”Punta Perpetua”, stands an imposing three-storey building dating back to the 19th century, currently in use as a nautical base. The upper level of the fortifications is formed by two salients on the west side, the salients of the ”Seven Winds”.

Nicosia is the divided capital city of the Republic of Cyprus. The northern part of the city (North Nicosia) is still under Turkish occupation, so Nicosia is the only remaining divided capital in Europe. It is situated on the banks of the River Pedieos and constitutes Cyprus’ financial capital and main international business center. The historic center of Nicosia today is located within the great medieval walls built by the Venetians. These walls are a trademark of the city, with its bastions and gates used to house important city buildings such as the City Hall and other buildings.
Church of Panagia (Our Lady) tou Moutoulla

The Odeon of Herodus Atticus (Herodeion) was the last monumental edifice to be built in antiquity (161 AD) in the Acropolis area and its construction was funded by Herodes Atticus in memory of his Roman wife Aspasia Anna Regillia. It was used mainly as a venue for music events and had a capacity of at least 5,000 people. It lasted intact until it was destroyed by the Heruli in 267 AD. The niches on the walls are now vacant, but in antiquity they used to house statues. The audience stands and the orchestra (stage) were restored using Pentelic marble in the 1950s and the monument has since hosted several cultural events, mainly in the context of the Athens Festival which runs from May through October each year, featuring a variety of acclaimed Greek as well as International performances

The Old Fortress of Corfu is one of the most impressive fortifications in Europe. The Old Fortress was constructed by the Venetians in the 15th century and was connected to the land by a movable, wooden bridge. In 1819, the British replaced this bridge with the present stable pathway, which is 60 m long and stands 15 m above the fosse. On the eastern side of the fortress there is the church of Saint George, built by the Venetians according to the Doric style. Two stone stairs lead to a high spot, where there is a beautiful polygonal well of 1732. The highest point of the fortress needs about 20 minutes walking up to a tall clock tower.

The Palacio de la Alajferia, from the era of Los Reinos de Tafas in the 11th century, is one of the best-preserved Muslim fortresses in Spain. Initially, the name was \'Palacio de la Alegría\' because it was built as a recreational residence for the Muslim kings. In its thousand years of history, however, the Palacio has also been a prison of the Inquisition, the Palacio de los Reyes Catolicos, and a barracks. Since 2001, it has been named Patrimonio de la Humanidad el arte mudéjar de Aragón by UNESCO. The tower that stands out on the wall is Torre del Trovador, a relatively recent name that owes its origins to the legend that inspired A. G. Gutiérrez\'s \'El Trovador\'.

Paleopolis is the area of ancient Corfu, located at the southeastern end of the city . The habitation in Paleopolis, which was the core of the ancient city of Corfu, begins at the end of the 8th century BC, when the Corinthian settlers arrived in the area. It was then abandoned in the Middle Ages, due to its destruction by barbaric raids, and its inhabitants founded the modern city of Corfu. The ancient city extends from the Halikiopoulos lake to the west and reaches the bay of Garitsa to the east. At the eastern end of the ancient market the visitor meets part of the ancient port facilities, while further south is a bath complex of Roman times (the best preserved building of the time in the area).

The Panathenaic Stadium of Athens, or Kallimarmaro, which hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896, is located on the site of an ancient Greek Stadium and for many centuries hosted the organization of gymnastic games, athletics as we would say today. Its history dates back to 330 BC and it is considered the oldest operating stadium in the world with an age of over 2300 years. It is also the only stadium in the world in which three Olympic Games have been held to date (1896, 1906, 2004), and the only one in the world that is made entirely of white Penteli marble from quarries opened exclusively for its construction.

Paphos is a city in the southwestern part of Cyprus, the capital of the province of the same name and one of the most important ancient kingdoms of the island. Among other things, it was also famous as a center of worship of the goddess Aphrodite. The city is divided into two levels: Upper Paphos, also known as Ktima, which is the commercial center of the city, and Kato Paphos, which is located lower and along the beaches and is the island\'s tourist destination. The entire archaeological site of Paphos has been under the protection of UNESCO since 1980.

Paphos Castle was originally a Byzantine fortress built to protect the port. The original Byzantine fortress was destroyed in the earthquake of 1222. It was rebuilt and expanded by the Lusignans in the 13th century. It is a castle consisting of a complex of two towers, the ruins of which are located 80 meters east of the Castle, right at the entrance of the port. The towers were destroyed after a strong earthquake in 1491, but their ruins are still visible. Nowadays, the castle is used as a tourist attraction and occasionally has thematic exhibitions.
Archaeological Park of Kato Paphos (Nea Paphos)
Archaeological Park of Kato Paphos (Nea Paphos)

Kato Paphos Archaeological Park (also Nea Paphos Archaeological Park) contains the major part of the important ancient Greek and Roman city and is located in Paphos, southwest Cyprus. Nea Paphos is one of the three components forming the Paphos archaeological complex inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1980 for its outstanding mosaics and ancient remains, as well as its historical religious importance. The archaeological site is still being excavated since it is widely believed that there are many treasures still to be discovered.

Patras is the largest city in the Peloponnese and the third largest in Greece, after Athens and Thessaloniki, with a population of 173.600 inhabitants, while the population of the Municipality of Patras is 215.922 inhabitants according to the 2021 census.

The wider metropolitan area includes approximately 305,000 inhabitants. Patras is the capital of the Regional Unit of Achaia, the Region of Western Greece, and the seat of the municipality of the same name.

The Castle of Patras is located on the foothills of Mount Panachaiko. Its foundation dates back to the 6th century AD during the reign of Justinian. Its construction was carried out with building material from the ancient Acropolis, which was located on the same spot and had already collapsed. The history of the castle is long and closely linked to the history of the city. The Castle of Patras consists of a wide outer enclosure with towers and bastions, surrounded on three sides by a deep moat. In the northeast corner, where a natural embankment rises, there is a second (inner) enclosure with strong towers, also protected by a moat. From 1950 to 1975 the castle belonged to the Municipality of Patreon and then it was granted to the Ministry of Culture - 6th Ephorate of Byzantine Antiquities and operates as an archaeological site. The interior of the castle appears today flattened and tree-lined, with no obvious traces of the buildings that once existed (temples, mosques, barracks, etc.). However, no systematic excavation has been carried out to date, in order to reveal the traces of the long history of the site, which dates back to ancient times.

The Obradoiro, the pilgrimage center of Santiago de Compostela the monumental center of Santiago de Compostela witnesses the history of an ancient city: Plaza del Obradoiro (a word that describes the workplace of the craftsmen) is one of the most beautiful and renowned squares in Spain and the monumental center of the an ancient city of Santiago de Compostela. It comprises several emblematic buildings of the city, spectators of its long history, that fuse different architectural styles of various epochs, such as Baroque, Gothic, Renaissance or neoclassical, collecting the cultural legacy of more than 700 years of history.

The Rio–Antirrio Bridge , officially the Charilaos Trikoupis Bridge, is one of the world\'s longest multi-span cable-stayed bridges and longest of the fully suspended type. It crosses the Gulf of Corinth near Patras, linking the town of Rio on the Peloponnese peninsula to Antirrio on mainland Greece by road. It opened one day before the Athens 2004 Summer Olympics, on 12 August 2004, and was used to transport the Olympic flame.

The Roman Odeon is located on the west side of Patra. It was built before the visit of Pausanias who rated it with the odeon of Herodes Atticus in Athens, as the most impressive of all the Odeons in Greece. It was rediscovered in 1889, and has been heavily restored since, including the new marble seating. The Odeon of Ancient Patrai was severely destroyed by successive invasions, wars and earthquakes. It was almost buried under the remains of other buildings and ground.

The Odeon seats approximately 2300 spectators. After the establishment of the Patra International Festival held during the summer months, the Ancient Odeon constitutes the main venue, welcoming many top Greek and foreign performers.

The impressive Rotunda, a domed circular building of the 4th century, is one of the UNESCO World Heritage Sites (since 1988) in Thessaloniki. The Rotunda belongs to the pericentric buildings and owes its name to its circular shape. It was built during the reign of Caesar Galerius, around 306 AD, as a temple of Zeus or Cabeir or, in other cases, as his Mausoleum. The magnificent monument is 29.80 metres high, 24.50 metres in diameter and the width of the walls is 6.30 metres. The lower part of the inner wall is formed in eight rectangular niches with arches decorated with mosaics. The interior of the monument impresses with the feeling of a large space with a huge dome.

In the southern coastal area of Patras, near the place of the martyrdom of Apostle Andrew, there are two churches dedicated to the patron saint of the city, the newest of which is one of the largest in the Balkans and is today the cathedral - symbol of Patras. The old temple was originally built at the end of the 5th century on the ruins of an ancient temple of Demeter. Architecturally, it belongs to the type of the three-aisled basilica. In the south aisle is the tomb of Agios Andreas, lined with marble, while next to the church, in an underground vaulted cave, there is a water spring, which is considered a holy water source. To the left of the old church is the imposing new church, in Byzantine style.

It was founded in 1908 by King George I and inaugurated in 1974, after its construction was interrupted due to the instability of the ground and financial problems. Its dome is 46 metres high and on its roof is a five-metre-high gilded cross, while smaller crosses crown the domes of the twelve bell towers. The interior has an area of 2,500 square metres and a capacity of more than 8,000 people. In the church is kept the casket of St. Andrew, which was given to Patras from Italy in 1964, as well as part of the cross of his martyrdom. The church celebrates on 30 November and on the Sunday closest to 26 September (the anniversary of the re-collection of the Holy Cara).

The Basilica of San Francesco is to be found in Assisi, in Umbria, along with other Franciscan sites. The basilica was built under the direction of Brother Elias, vicar general and architect of the order, starting in 1228, just two years after the saint\'s death, as a place designed to receive his remains. It is built into the side of a hill and comprises two churches (known as the Upper Church and the Lower Church) and a crypt, where the remains of the saint are interred. The Upper and Lower Churches are decorated with frescoes by numerous late medieval painters from the Roman and Tuscan schools.

The Basilica of San Biagio, located on Maratea\'s highest point, houses the patron saint\'s remains. Its origins are unclear, but it likely started as a Basilian monastery that later became a church in 732 AD when it housed Saint Blaise\'s relics. The strategic location led to military fortifications under the Lombards and became the first refuge for Blanda\'s inhabitants, forming Maratea\'s initial community.

Legend tells of Saint Blaise\'s relics arriving during the 8th-century iconoclastic persecutions, accompanied by a dazzling halo visible to Maratea\'s residents. The Sanctuary witnessed the miracle of the Manna, water flowing from the relic urn, collected and distributed to the needy. On May 3, 1941, the Sanctuary gained Basilica status.

Tamassos was a city-kingdom in ancient Cyprus, one of the ten kingdoms of Cyprus. The city-state prospered mainly because of its mines, from which metals (mostly copper, Cyprus\'s chief export in the ancient world) were extracted. Sporadic excavations between 1970 and 1990 in the outer area resulted in the discovery of many artifacts as well as parts of the original city dating from the Archaic, Classical, and Hellenistic eras. The visible sections of this large and important archaeological site also include the site of the temple of Aphrodite, the two majestic royal tombs, and other graves.

The Roman Theatre in Cartagena was built during the Roman period, specifically in the 1st century BC. It was part of the Roman city of Carthago Nova, a significant port city during the Roman Empire. The theater served as a venue for theatrical performances, including plays, musicals, and other cultural events. The Roman Theatre remained buried and undiscovered for centuries until its excavation in the 1980s. The restoration work aimed to uncover and preserve the theater\'s remains, allowing visitors to experience its historical significance. Today, the restored theater stands as a prominent cultural and archaeological site in Cartagena.

The Temple of Minerva is an ancient Roman building, situated in the very city centre in Assisi. It was built during the first century and then converted into the church of Santa Maria della Minerva in 1539. It was renovated in the 17th century in the Baroque style, but the façade is still the original Roman columns and architrave dating back to the first century BC.

The Sassi quarters, a World Heritage Site since 1993, feature houses, churches, and monasteries built in natural caves of the Murgia, spanning 1,016 hectares. Inhabited from Palaeolithic to the Iron Age, it expanded beyond Roman-era defensive walls around Civita, its first core. Early houses were simple caves enclosed by walls from quarried blocks. Christianity influenced its history, leading to the construction of places of worship during the Middle Ages. Relocated in the 1950s for improvements, the population returned in the 1980s, restoring traditional use of the Sassi.

Thessaloniki is the most important administrative, cultural and business centre in northern Greece, and the second largest city in Greece. A medium-sized city located on the sea, with a population of over 1.1 million in its metropolitan area. It is bordered by the Aegean Sea, an hour from Mount Olympus and half an hour from magnificent beaches, with a short flight from the capitals of the Balkan, Mediterranean and all of Europe.

The Tombs of the Kings is a large necropolis lying about two kilometers north of Paphos harbor in Cyprus. In 1980, it was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The underground tombs, many of which date back to the 4th century BC, are carved out of solid rock, and are thought to have been the burial sites of Paphitic aristocrats and high officials up to the third century AD. Some of the tombs feature Doric columns and frescoed walls. Archaeological excavations are still being carried out at the site.

The White Tower of Thessaloniki is an Ottoman fortification of the 15th century (probably built between 1450-70). Today it is considered a characteristic monument of Thessaloniki and is all that has survived from the demolished Ottoman fortification of the city. The White Tower is a cylindrical structure 33,9 metres high and 22,7 metres in diameter. It has six floors, 34 metres high and 70 metres in circumference, which are connected by an internal staircase, which is spiral-shaped and in contact with the outer wall. Today it serves as a museum and is one of the most famous city-symbol buildings in Greece overlooking the beach of Thessaloniki.

The Woods of San Francesco, a path of 64 hectares and 800 years of history, stretches for two and a half kilometres among hornbeam, oak trees, forest land, farmland and ancient works of man. The route descends in hairpin bends towards the Tescio river and the Galli Bridge dating back to 1356, all the way to the valley floor where you can admire the remains of the complex of Santa Croce. What remains of the religious building are the renovated hospital facilities, the Romanesque church, the windmill and the tower, each one with its own history to remember and to tell.

Do you know a town called Cesaraugusta? No? Then perhaps you have heard of Zaragoza nowadays. Cesaraugusta, in honor of Emperor Caesar Augustus, is in fact the first name given to the city when the Romans first settled on the banks of the Ebro river in the 1st century. After the Romans, Zaragoza was the land of many peoples such as the Suebi and Visigoths, until the domination of the Arabs in the 8th century. In 1118, after being conquered by King Alfonso I el Batallador, the city became the capital of the Kingdom of Aragon. Today Zaragoza is the fifth most populous city in Spain and still the capital of Aragon.
